h1: Gin distillery licensing: the steps most places share
title: Gin Distillery Licensing: Common Steps | Craft Beer School
desc: The licensing steps most countries share for a gin distillery, from company set-up to premises, excise registration and labels, in a workable order.
teaser: Licences set your launch date more often than equipment does. Know the steps and their order before you commit money.
standfirst: Rules differ by country and by Indian state. They also change. The shape of the process is similar almost everywhere. Learn the shape, then check the details with the regulator.
sections:
A distillery cannot sell a bottle without permission. The permissions arrive on the regulator's timetable. Money spent on equipment and premises before the licence route is clear is money at risk.

This guide gives the common sequence. It is not legal advice and it gives no fees or section numbers. Rules differ by country and, in India, by state, because alcohol is a state subject. Always check the current notification with the regulator or a licensing adviser.
Steps one and two: the business and the premises

Register the legal entity that will hold the licences. Open a bank account, get tax registrations and settle who the owners and directors are. Regulators often check the people behind a licence, so keep ownership records clear and complete.

Most regulators approve the premises before a licence is granted. Expect questions on location, zoning, building safety, fire protection, storage of spirit, effluent and security. A site near a school or place of worship may face restrictions in some places.

Choose premises with the licence in mind. A lease signed before the use is confirmed can leave you paying rent on a building you cannot use. Ask a licensing adviser to check the site before you commit.
Step three: the manufacture or distillery licence

The core licence permits you to make spirit or to blend and bottle it. The category may differ if you distil from neutral spirit, rectify, bottle or only own a brand and use a contract maker. A contract arrangement needs the right permissions on both sides. See how contract-distilled gin works.

Applications usually need plans of the premises, equipment lists and a description of the process. Keep the documents consistent with your project report.
Steps four and five: duty and labels

Spirits are taxed almost everywhere. You will usually need to register for excise or duty, keep stock and production records and file returns. Some jurisdictions use bonded storage so duty is paid when stock leaves. Set up your record keeping from the first day, not after the first inspection.

Many places require labels to be approved before sale. Rules cover the mandatory text, strength statement, volume, producer details and warnings. They differ by country and Indian state. Do not print a large label run before approval. Selling in several states or countries means several approvals, each on its own timeline.
Step six: selling and moving the product

Selling needs more permissions. You may need permits to transport spirit, registrations with state distributors or bodies and a licence to sell at your own shop or online. Online sales of alcohol are restricted or banned in many places. Check before you build a shop page. See selling gin direct for how this affects direct sales.
After the licence: records, costs and advisers

Getting the licence is the start of the obligation. Most regulators expect accurate records of spirit received, spirit made, stock held and bottles sold. Many inspect premises and stock. Keep records up to date and in a form that someone else can read.

A distiller who treats record keeping as a weekly habit finds an inspection dull. One who treats it as a chore finds it stressful. Choose the first. Use a simple stock register, count physical stock against it regularly and keep the paperwork for each batch.

Do not guess fees, because they change and vary. Instead, budget three things: adviser time, application costs as quoted by the regulator today and the cost of waiting. The cost of waiting is rent, salaries and loan interest while the plant stands idle. Put it in your cash flow with a pessimistic delay. A licence that arrives early is a pleasant surprise. One that arrives late should not sink the plan.

A good licensing adviser knows the local office, the forms and the usual sticking points. Ask what they have done for distilleries, not only for retail. Agree what is included, who files what and how you will be updated. Keep your own copy of every application and receipt.

Do not hand over responsibility. The licence is in your name. The inspector will ask you the questions.
Plan the timeline and stay honest about it
Build the licence steps into your schedule with a wide margin. Do not promise a launch date to partners or investors until the key approvals are in hand. We cannot promise a licence. Nobody else can.
faqs: It varies widely by country and Indian state. Ask the regulator and a local adviser. Leave a wide buffer.
Do I need a licence if a contract distillery makes my gin?
Often you need some permission as the brand owner, plus label approval and sales registration. Check the rules where you sell.
Not everywhere. Many places restrict or ban online alcohol sales. Check first.
Who should I ask for help?
The regulator for the rules and a licensing adviser or lawyer for your case. This guide is not legal advice.
